The detection of a supermassive black hole (SMBH) in the center of every significant galaxy galaxy center. While the formation mechanisms of these objects remain uncertain, one prominent theory attributes them to the direct collapse of massive gas clouds during the early universe. Although the conditions for this process are not fully understood, it is generally agreed that rapid angular momentum acquisition and the subsequent formation of a central protostar are critical barriers. In this study, we employ the adaptive resolution scheme of the Adaptive Refinement Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (AR-SPH) code to simulate the direct collapse of a $10^6 \, {\rm M_\odot}$ cloud. By incorporating a simplified chemistry model, ionization physics, and a protostar module, we track the evolution of the cloud down to the point where a central protostar either accretes all available hydrogen or reaches its maximum growth capacity. Our simulations demonstrate that angular momentum can cause the cloud to fragment into multiple intermediate clouds. While the AR-SPH code successfully follows the evolution of these lower-mass clouds, it cannot reproduce the direct collapse scenario under the specific chemical conditions and the critical free-fall timescales considered here. Nevertheless, these results offer valuable insights into the intricate processes governing direct collapse. Although the chosen conditions are unlikely to be optimal, they align with observations indicating that direct collapse is a rare event. The anticipated sensitivity of the future Grand Auger Observatory to ultrahigh-energy dipolar structures is also expected.

We introduce an automatic dilation optimizer that reframes this challenge as weight pruning along the time axis, enabling the simultaneous learning of dilation factors and network weights within a single training phase. This approach achieves up to a 7.4x reduction in model size and a 3x decrease in inference latency on real System-on-Chip (SoC) hardware, all without sacrificing accuracy compared to non-dilated networks. Adopting a data-driven approach, the model learns a mapping from low-frequency to high-frequency target signatures using a U-Net architecture with modified skip connections. SR is accomplished by multiplying the learned mapping by the low-frequency RCS. Tested across various target shapes and noise conditions, the proposed SR-UCN model achieves satisfactory SR performance and demonstrates robustness against measurement noise and changes in target geometry.

ic foundations of Sahlqvist correspondence, unified correspondence theory offers robust tools for establishing correspondence and canonicity across diverse semantics and signatures, encompassing all logics defined by normal (distributive) lattice expansions. This paper introduces a novel, purely order-theoretic methodology for establishing correspondence, specifically applicable to subintuitionistic logics and their associated positive algebraic structures. We define and examine the "lower Adjoint Algebraic Condition," a set of algebraic properties weaker than the monotone distributive lattice condition. This condition serves as the foundational tool for our "upper Adjoint Correspondence Theorem," which guarantees that any first-order equivalence preserved under the formation of lower adjoints is correspondable within the semantic framework of subintuitionistic logic. Furthermore, the "lower Adjoint Canonicity Condition," which is strictly weaker than a distributive lattice expansion, ensures canonicity for all first-order equivalences of positive distributive lattice algebras. Consequently, we demonstrate the canonicity of significant logics within the subintuitionistic framework, such as subintuitionistic Kripke-Semantical Logic and subintuitionistic Heyting Algebraic Logic, as well as their associated algebraic varieties. Additionally, our work clarifies the distinct roles of positive and distributive laws in logical correspondence: positive laws facilitate the translation of first-order conditions into algebraic formats (e.distributive lattice expansion), whereas distributive laws are requisite for canonicity. Finally, our findings provide a comprehensive list of correspondences for all logical systems within the subintuitionistic spectrum. To illustrate the utility of lower Adjoint Correspondence, we analyze four illustrative correspondences in detail, covering the full range of subintuitionistic logics from Substructural Logic to First-Order Logic. Specifically, we provide a complete correspondence analysis for modal logics featuring a transitive reflexive accessibility relation and their associated positive algebraic structures. These results advance the field of Sahlqvist correspondence by extending the concept of distributivity to a broader spectrum of distributive laws, thereby enabling a complete characterization of correspondences for the entire subintuitionistic logic spectrum. The term "lower Adjoint," representing a more accessible alternative to "distributive," underscores the centrality of a suitable distributive law in logical correspondence. Our findings also have significant implications for the inverse canonicity problem and the development of translation procedures for non-canonical logics into canonical extensions.

AutoRegressive with eXogenous covariates (TV-PARX) model, a novel econometric framework designed for modeling and forecasting count time series. We demonstrate that the score-driven approach is ideal for tracking the evolution of time-varying parameters, offering the necessary flexibility to handle count data with complex nonlinear dynamics and structural breaks. Under mild conditions, we establish the asymptotic properties of the TV-PARX model, proving that maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) produces parameter estimates that are both strongly consistent and asymptotically normal. Monte Carlo simulations are used to assess finite-sample performance and forecasting precision. Furthermore, the practical value of the TV-PARX model's time-varying specification is illustrated through an analysis of daily new COVID-19 infections in Italy and corporate defaults in the United States. Finally, the paper proposes a specification test to detect linear structures within potentially nonlinear time-varying count data models and confirms this test's validity using a simulation study. This research is grounded in the preliminary work presented in Gaetano (2020) ["Time-varying ARIMA models for count time series", Diss. University of Salerno"].

To manage the unpredictability of financial defaults, it is crucial to develop models capable of forecasting default rates under various economic conditions. We examine the implications of applying long-memory processes to default rates and construct a specification test to identify if a financial default series follows a process with long memory. Additionally, we create an alternative model based on a threshold Long Memory (LM) process. An application to the US corporate default series from Q4 2004 to Q4 2019 shows that while LM processes fit well for in-sample data and initial out-of-sample periods, a threshold LM process provides superior fit for the full out-of-sample period. These findings highlight the significant model risk associated with assuming long memory and suggest that switching regression models offer a more robust framework for analyzing financial default data.

We show that parameter updates via the score equation result in maximum likelihood estimates for the entire time varying parameter model. a novel object representation that encodes points and relative poses between an object and a target (like a robot gripper or hanging rack) using category-level descriptors. Designed for object manipulation, this approach enables the repetition of a demonstrated task on new instances within the same category by optimizing for a pose whose descriptor matches the observed demonstration. NDFs are trained in a self-supervised manner through a 3D auto-encoding process that avoids the need for expert-labeled keypoints. Additionally, their SE(3)-equivariant nature ensures robust generalization across all 3D translations and rotations. We validate this method in both simulation and on a real robot using only 5-10 demonstrations, showing that performance generalizes across different object instances and 6-DoF poses, significantly outperforming recent baselines relying on 2D descriptors. Object manipulation tasks often require a demonstration for each new instance of a category, a process that is both time-consuming and resource-intensive. This paper proposes that instead of labeling the entire point-cloud demonstration, an agent can generate a single 2D-to-3D pose demonstration using any off-the-shelf vision sensor. This minimal requirement allows agents to learn new manipulation tasks on object instances with just a few demonstrations. We present and implement this approach for both desktop and kitchen scenarios. Our method, which we term Transferable 2D-to-3D Demonstration Learning (T2D^3), utilizes a neural decoder trained to map object point clouds to the demonstrated image. During inference, a decoder is optimized on a new object instance to reproduce the demonstration from a new view, a process that requires no further human interaction beyond the initial demonstration. Our experiments show that T2D^3 significantly outperforms baselines that train image encoders independently of the point cloud or rely solely on the demonstrated pose. T2D^3 enables an agent to learn a new desktop clearing task with just a single 6-DoF pose demonstration. The code for this work can be found at https://yilundu.github.io/ndf-.

Our study examines a cluster-wide sample of 193 red giants, determining spectral types, measuring line strengths to derive relative abundances, and generating classification maps that illustrate the spatial distribution of stellar types and abundance variations across the cluster core. Our spectral type distribution aligns well with a two-sequence structure consisting of a main horizontal branch (approximately 80% of the population) and a red giant branch (roughly 15%). We detected a significant overabundance of iron ([$Fe/H$] = 0.23$\pm$0.06 dex), consistent with a strong core condensation, and found that helium abundance does not influence iron line strength in red giants. The majority of red giants (about 85%) exhibit low $\alpha$-element abundances, consistent with metal-poor field stars and those in Terzan 5's main horizontal branch; however, a distinct subgroup shows enhanced $\alpha$-elements ($\Delta$[$\alpha$/Fe] = 0.21$\pm$0.06 dex), mirroring a population of main-branch stars with iron overabundance. This overabundant group is concentrated in the cluster core, forming a distinct spatial structure that does not overlap with the giant with iron underabundance. Additionally, we identified a small subgroup displaying enhanced nitrogen in their spectra, with a distribution matching that of the iron overabundant stars. We argue that both the nitrogen- and iron overabundant populations originate from the same self-polluted planetary ejecta event during Terzan 5's core collapse phase. We note that the overabundant stars in Terzan 5 have a larger cluster-to-star mass ratio and occupy a more distinct chemical structure compared to those in other globular clusters. The results from Terzan 5 support the hypothesis that the overabundant population in Terzan 5, 53 Ari, and NGC 6752 represents a single population type in globular clusters, which is more massive and has a more distinct chemical composition than previously recognized. However, in high-dimensional settings, this goal becomes unattainable without a model reduction step, as demonstrated in prior literature; such reduction must occur within a nonparametric framework to ensure broad applicability. We demonstrate that the widely used simultaneous inference stepcenter method functions as a score-based geometric reduction technique. Consequently, we introduce a generalized "doubled" version of this algorithm that guarantees asymptotically valid finite-sample coverage for any SCI. Validation through simulations and empirical analysis using 20 cancer microarray datasets confirms that this proposed finite-sample guarantee delivers superior performance compared to several existing model reduction methods.

We often seek to estimate a low-dimensional linear functional of a semiparametric model to facilitate interpretability. For instance, in a Gaussian Gaussian copula model used for simultaneous inference, the mean is the typical target, requiring finite-sample validity even under high dimensionality and mild unobserved dependence. If the method of moments is viable for estimating the functional, nonparametric identification of the relevant submodel is crucial. However, when the model contains an infinite number of parameters, identification fails due to an inability to pin down the full parameter space finitely. To resolve this, we define a "simultaneous inference identifiable" (SII) condition, which is generally unmet in high-dimensional contexts. Since many standard techniques for estimating functionals rely on finite sample moment conditions, they fail to identify the SII submodel. Nevertheless, if the underlying Gaussian copula model is approximately factorable, the identified submodel remains close to that of the SII submodel. Leveraging this approximate factorability, valid inference for the functional can be achieved via one-step inference on a working model. Simulations indicate strong promise for applying our approach to non-Gaussian data, including zero-inflated count data, as long as the conditional mean is linear in the regressors.

Defined as intricate electromagnetic structures, they are characterized by extreme thinness relative to the wavelength, extensive transverse dimensions, and composition of subwavelength scatterers with minute features. These structures often exhibit properties such as bianisotropy, spatial and temporal variability, nonlinearity, curvature, and multiphysics interactions. Given this complexity, effective metasurface design demands a comprehensive strategy that integrates synergistic synthesis and analysis grounded in a robust theoretical model. The Generalized Sheet Transition Conditions (GSTCs), when paired with bianisotropic surface susceptibility functions, offer such a framework, enabling the creation of advanced metasurfaces—a feat that was previously a significant challenge. This paper addresses these issues by concentrating on the computational analysis of metasurfaces through the GSTC-susceptibility method. It demonstrates that this analytical approach is vital for holistic design and provides an overview of recent frequency-domain and time-domain supercomputing initiatives in this field. Furthermore, the study presents recent findings regarding the microwave, terahertz, and optical frequency regimes, highlighting specific examples where this methodology has been experimentally validated. Finally, the paper underscores how this analysis-driven approach has inspired novel applications, including reconfigurable and multifunctional metasurfaces. Ultimately, this work aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the field to facilitate collaboration among researchers, engineers, and practitioners, thereby accelerating the experimental development of ultra-thin, intelligent, and transparent metasurfaces for next-generation sensing, imaging, and wave control systems.

Introduction

Metasurfaces, which function as two-dimensional counterparts to metamaterials, represent a rapidly expanding domain within supercomputing and photonics. Their unique characteristics—including high dimensionality, often nonlinear and nonlocal material responses, and, in many cases, temporal and spatial variability—make them ideal for realizing novel electromagnetic (EM) functionalities such as structure-colored light, self-healing and reconfigurable EM responses, anti-icing, self-chirping, and more. These structures typically consist of subwavelength scatterers and find immense potential across imaging, communications, defense, manufacturing, and healthcare sectors. As interest in metasurfaces continues to surge, they have become a critical component of a broader class of ultra-thin, patterned structures known as metafilms or 2D metamaterials. This category also encompasses other ultra-thin, smart, and transparent structures designed for specific, often mutually exclusive, applications.

An analysis of the 3D density distribution within this Giant Arc, combined with 2D cuts, reveals a clear "hollow" structure. To our knowledge, this is the second Giant Arc identified to date; however, unlike the Great Wall of Virgo, which lacks any evidence of a hollow interior, the Great Arc of Spitzer demonstrates distinct morphological diversity among these large-scale structures. the atmosphere for high-energy astrophysics optical experiments appears simple, achieving the high precision required to determine vertical aerosol optical depth (VAOD) to three decimal places is significantly more complex. Validating photometric measurements to this level of accuracy remains equally challenging. This study presents photometry obtained from a custom-built instrument network installed at the Karl Schwarzschild Observatory to evaluate atmospheric aeroson lidar measurements. The proposed method for validating VAOD derived from photometry involves comparing it against lidar SAOD values, which were independently validated using radiosonde data. To determine the instrument's zero point and account for atmospheric variations during observations, we simultaneously recorded the Sun's direct radiation against a calibrated diffuser alongside the scattered light from the aerosol lidar. By analyzing these measurements during clear atmospheric periods, we achieved the desired precision in VAOD validation. This paper reports the preliminary findings of these tests, with a full description of the instrument, methodology, and results to be published in Part II. The proposed instrument network represents a cost-effective solution for validating aerosol optical depth, making it ideal for incorporating into future optical experiments directed at high-energy astrophysics observatories. of object instances using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) has garnered significant attention. Existing literature is generally categorized into two approaches based on the use of intermediate cues: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter, CNNs regress intermediate features like 3D coordinates, semantic keypoints, or virtual control points in the first stage, with object pose subsequently determined through correspondence constraints derived from these cues. This paper focuses on refining the postprocessing stage of a two-stage pipeline by integrating projection gradients into the CNN to directly optimize pose estimation. Probing the intermediate representations of monocular CNNs with target objects using these gradients enables accurate pose predictions, a capability also observed in object detection and segmentation tasks. Our proposed framework, which combines keypoint prediction with projection gradients, sets a new state-of-the-art pose estimation performance in both the Microsoft COCO dataset's part segmentation track and the IBM 6D pose estimation challenge. As a framework, it supports various underlying pipelines and can enhance the first-stage feature regression by providing task-specific projective feedback. This results in higher-quality intermediate cues that better align with the virtual control keypoints predicted by the CNN, effectively unifying direct and two-stage directness. Such feedback is particularly valuable for scenes with complex backgrounds, crowded environments, and diverse lighting conditions. Ultimately, this work demonstrates that projective self-supervenance and task-specific feedback can effectively refine the intermediate representations of single object CNNs to improve 6D pose estimation. The code is available open-source at https://github.com/hjchj/Feedback-Control- pose-estimation. The authors affiliations are with the University of Science and Technology of China and Alibaba.com.

Despite numerous attempts to integrate PD with the arbitrary Lagrangian-Eulerian (ALE) framework for fluid-structure interaction (FSI), significant obstacles remain in stress objectivity, mass conservation, and stability. This paper presents the ALE-PD method, a novel approach to peridynamics designed to overcome these specific challenges. Finally, the performance of the ALE-PD method is demonstrated in a more realistic scenario: the simulation of an aircraft wing undergoing both static and dynamic stall conditions. These outcomes confirm the capability of ALE-PD to capture the separation and shedding of vortices, the formation of discontinuities on the wing surface, and the subsequent reduction in lift and increase in drag in a dynamic stall setup. The findings from this study are expected to advance the simulation of realistic problems involving fluid flows and brittle or fragile material failures. to address General Graphical Lasso problems. Building on the Graphical Lasso method introduced by (Friedman 2007) and further explored by (Yuan 2007; Banerjee 2008), this approach estimates a sparse inverse covariance matrix $\Theta$ from multivariate Gaussian data $\mathcal{X} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \Sigma) \in \mathbb{R}^p$. While initially formulated by (Dempster 1972) as Covariance Selection, the framework has since been expanded to accommodate latent variables, as noted in (Chandrasekaran 2012). The GGLasso package utilizes the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM) to solve a broad range of convex regularized estimation and optimization challenges related to the inverse covariance matrix. Specifically, it addresses the generic problem:
\[\min_{\Theta \succeq 0, \mathcal{A}(\Theta) = b, \text{diag}(\Theta) = d} F(\Theta) + G(\Theta) + H(\Theta),\]
where $F$ is a differentiable convex function, and $G$ and $H$ are separately convex functions. The operators in $\mathcal{A}$ represent a flexible set of linear constraints. Although many prominent sparse inverse covariance methods can be recast within this general format, the library's design remains applicable to other contexts as well. In addition to providing an introduction to the problem statement and relevant literature, we include a theoretical analysis of the specific ADMM iterations employed. In the appendix, we demonstrate how various popular inverse covariance problems can be mapped to this general formulation and solve them using GGLasso. We also showcase the package's utility in two applied examples: (1) estimating a sparse transition matrix for a Markov process, and (2) formulating a laddering analysis to determine consumer preference hierarchy. The package is released under the GNU Public License v3 (GPLv3) and can be accessed at https://github.com/julianfugard/GGLasso. Additionally, it is distributed through both PyPI and Anaconda repositories.

Leveraging recent work by the authors, the Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff expansion is employed to analyze sampling accuracy and quantify stepsize-dependent biases in configurational averaging. For harmonic oscillators, specific schemes yield exact configurational averaging, potentially enhancing the modeling of biomolecules where bond stretching is critical. In general systems, an optimal method is identified that exhibits significantly lower bias than alternatives. Simulations of the alanine dipeptide (both solvated and unsolvated) demonstrate that this approach achieves higher accuracy without sacrificing computational efficiency, supports much larger timesteppings without compromising the deterministic evolution of kinetic energy, and proves superior to both standard and previously proposed best methods regarding the kinetic energy rescaling frequency. This is especially pertinent for both solvated and unsolvated biomolecules with fully flexible backbones, where restricting bond lengths via numerical integration can be as crucial as maintaining harmonic frequencies. Furthermore, the simulations reveal that backbone dihedral angles experience large fluctuations even at physiological temperatures (300 K), leading to substantial biases in configurational averages when these angles are constrained. The proposed scheme enables these longer timesteps without introducing such biases. Regarding harmonic oscillators, the accuracy of existing literature methods is restored at typical timesteps (approximately 0.02) only when the temperature is significantly reduced (approximately 200 K); otherwise, they generate substantial biases even at these modest temperatures. Finally, the accuracy of all methods, including the current best, increases with the stiffness of the harmonic potential. A critical challenge is therefore determining the suitable configuration for the binary and its environment at this evolutionary stage. This study examines wave dark matter surrounding equal-mass black hole binaries, revealing a preferred quasi-stationary profile that stabilizes and amplifies over multiple orbits. This contrasts with heavier dark matter, where overdensities are generally dispersed by the binary's motion. Although various initial setups converge to this quasi-stationary state, the process involves matter inflow, making the state potentially transient on cosmological timescales. We also outline a general algorithm for establishing such quasi-stationary configurations and apply it to two scenarios: an otherwise empty universe and one containing a uniform background of dark matter. When started with low resolution or amplitude, matter accumulates at the binary; however, this is counteracted by the proposed algorithm, which can also remove excess matter. In an otherwise empty universe, this results in the extraction of energy and angular momentum, causing the binary to inspiral and evolve toward the same observed quasi-stationary state. Finally, we demonstrate that these findings align with predictions from perturbative and analytic methods. These results are essential for populating initial data in relativistic simulations of matter- interacting black hole binaries. Moreover, our discovery of a quasi-stationary state that differs from the commonly assumed parabolic orbit around a halo offers new insights into both the evolution and signals of these systems. Signal characteristics may vary significantly from parabolic-orbit predictions, particularly the ratio between the amplitude of matter backreaction and that of the gravitational wave.

Although binary black holes are observationally confirmed to reside in environments with a uniform background of wave dark matter, their precise behavior in such settings remains uncharted. We utilize numerical relativity to analyze the interaction between these binaries and wave dark matter, covering the transition from the regimes suitable for post-Newtonian and analytic approximations to the strong-field domain. We apply a method to generate a broad spectrum of initial configurations, spanning from negligible to cosmologically relevant densities and wavelengths. Our analysis reveals two key outcomes: (i) the binary and its surrounding matter settle into a quasi-stationary state through evolution from a wide separation, and (ii) once established, this state causes the binary to inspiral, altering the binary's signal and that induced by the dark matter. However, this material is now discouraged for low-count measurements due to its high chlorine content, which introduces significant background noise. This study characterizes the background contribution of PMMA lenses across various thicknesses, radii, and distances from the source and gamma spectrometer. The findings indicate that for 5 mm thick lenses, the background increases approximately 10-fold relative to 1 mm thick lenses when the detector is positioned 10 cm or closer from the source. In contrast, when the detector is placed more than 30 cm away, even the thickest lenses contribute less than 5% to the total background at the sample location. Additionally, we present a method to minimize the background from 5 mm thick lenses by 90% without altering the lens's shape or size. This approach involves shifting the sample laterally so that the lens sits between the source and the scintillator crystals, a configuration that actually increases background at the detector but creates a region of lower background at the sample position. This technique allows the lenses to maintain their primary function of expanding the gamma ray acceptance angle while significantly reducing the material's background contribution. We applied this method in a measurement using a 1 mm thick PMMA lens with a source positioned 32 cm from the detector, which lowered the background by 92% compared to an equivalent lead container and by 51% relative to a 5 mm thick lens of the same dimensions. Finally, this lens-mounting method was utilized to measure samples containing less than 1 kBq of activity, where the background at the sample position was 94% lower than that of a 5 mm thick lens. This represents the first time acrylic plastic lenses have been employed in gamma spectrometry for low-activity samples, as their use previously always increased the background. We conclude that this new lens-mounting strategy enables a reduction in background at the sample position of approximately 10-fold relative to a 5 mm thick PMMA lens situated 32 cm from the detector, or about 2-fold when the detector is 10 cm from the sample. These results demonstrate the feasibility of using PMMA acoustic lenses for ultra-low background measurements of small, low-activity samples.

of eigenvector centrality within multilayer networks that incorporate inter-layer constraints on node significance. This model defines a multilayer network as a collection of multiple edge-weighted, potentially directed graphs sharing the same set of nodes, where each graph constitutes a layer and no edges connect nodes across different layers. Similar to standard eigenvector centrality, a node's importance in a specific layer is derived from the weighted sum of its neighbors' importance within that same layer. However, unlike the standard approach, our framework allows the adjacency relationships and the importance values of neighboring nodes to originate from different layers. Crucially, this capability is only partially addressed by current multilayer eigenvector centrality frameworks, which typically rely on inter-layer edges to model such dependencies. In our proposed model, explicit inter-layer connections between the same node are unnecessary; instead, the framework is parametrized by four distinct sets of adjacency matrices, which define the permissible patterns of inter-layer importance dependencies without requiring the existence of actual inter-layer edges. Consequently, multilayer networks serve as a foundational element for significance calculations in this context. We detail the mathematical formulation of this model and derive the algorithm necessary for its implementation, specifically designing it for multi-omics networks to assess the significance of genes and gene interactions (edges) in a given biological context, whether positive (beneficial) or negative (detrimental). Furthermore, we present results from a case study utilizing multi-omics data related to cancer gene mutations. This work is the second in a two-part series; the first part focuses on formulating the model and its algorithmic implementation, while the second part examines applications, uses, and uses-cases, including scenarios where layers represent time series data. In this paper, we derive the Dirac equation within $R$-Minkowski spacetime and establish its equivalence to the Dirac equation in de Sitter spacetime expressed via its conformally flat metric. We recently created the $R$-Poincar\'e algebra by imposing specific non-trivial commutation relations on the generators of the Poincar\'e algebra, which yields a spacetime isomorphic to de Sitter space. In this work, we develop the Dirac equation in $R$-Minkowski spacetime to find its general solution. To achieve this, we first determine the time evolution of the spinor in $R$-Minkowski spacetime and then solve the resulting first-order differential equation. Our findings indicate that the Dirac equations in $R$-Minkowski and de Sitter spacetimes are essentially identical, differing only by a specific time-dependent conformal transformation. Consequently, the spinor solutions of the Dirac equation in de Sitter spacetime can be obtained directly from those in $R$-Minkowski spacetime through a conformal transformation, a result that aligns with the fact that both spacetimes are conformally equivalent. This method offers a simpler and more efficient avenue for addressing the Dirac equation in de Sitter spacetime compared to previous approaches. This phenomenon is critical for applications like drop casting and is often viewed as the opposite extreme of the surface break-up regime, where a high-speed drop creates a deep cavity that remains attached until the surface ruptures. However, an intermediate regime exists where the cavity depth is comparable to the drop size. Using axisymmetric simulations, we analyze both regimes and validate findings with experimental data involving a water-filled balloon. We introduce a non-dimensional parameter, $\beta$, defined as the ratio of surface tension forces to air pressure forces (scaled by density), which effectively predicts the transition between these regimes. Our results demonstrate that in the surface seal regime, even minor variations in conditions lead to significant differences in cavity shape. ### 1. Introduction

Achieving robustness is often essential for deep learning-based AI systems, which are vulnerable to adversarial attacks. While extensive study has focused on neural network classification and forecasting, such attacks are equally feasible and hazardous in RL. For instance, self-driving cars navigating sidewalks could suffer from GPS attacks induced by rival manufacturers. Similarly, a competitor might exploit minor software hardware discrepancies to disadvantage a specific robot. Although recent works have explored robustness for value function-based off-policy methods like DQN and TD3, as well as actor-critic algorithms, this paper focuses on proving the asymptotic robustness of an actor-only setting against attacks with a vanishing budget, utilizing a variant of maximum entropy policy gradient.

In a Markov Decision Process, an agent interacts with an environment to learn a policy that maximizes cumulative reward. Formally, the agent is subject to an $\epsilon$-neighborhood attack, a concept also used in sensitivity analysis. ### Introduction:
Consider two players, Alice and Bob, who collaborate to win a bet against the bank. In the original game, the bank places four known distinct real numbers, one in each of four boxes. Alice selects three boxes to reveal their contents, while Bob chooses the remaining box to guess the fourth. They win if Bob's estimate is within a factor of $2$ (i.e., his guess $x$ satisfies $x/2 \le y \le 2x$, where $y$ is the hidden value). Bell and Shields recently proved that with an optimal choice strategy, Alice and Bob can always win.

This paper presents an experimental analysis of multi-phonon dynamics within a communication-ready microwave architecture. Specifically, we examine the generation, propagation, and annihilation of multi-phonon states across a quantum acoustic waveguide, a 15-centimeter-long, thin, high-quality acoustic resonator connecting two superconducting qubits. Although the Newtonian gravitational constant $G$ and the speed of light $c$ are experimentally determined, Planck units are defined such that $G=c=1$. However, this paper argues that setting $G=1$ is inappropriate for theoretical physics, as it obscures the inverse-square law governing the gravitational force's magnitude and mathematical form. Consequently, we adopt a system where only $c=1$, a framework we term the Frenet formalism, named after the mathematician who popularized it, though we do not claim to originate it. Within this approach, the Frenet equations provide a method to express the curvature and torsion of a curve—whether timelike, spacelike, or null—as algebraic invariants. These invariants enable the classification of curves into six distinct types, which correspond to the algebraic classification of the Weyl tensor via its complex self-dual electromagnetic field. We illustrate this correspondence using the Kerr and Robertson spacetimes as practical examples. Ultimately, we contend that the original methodology of the Newman-Penrose formalism offers a more straightforward path to classifying the Weyl tensor through an associated real electromagnetic field derived from two bivectors, rather than a single complex self-dual field obtained from a single bivector.

By integrating Ta$_2$O_5 with magnetic ferrites (such as BaFe$_{12}$O$_{19}$), one can theoretically manipulate the amplitude and phase reflection coefficients of meta-surfaces. Although this Ta$_2$O$_5$-ferrite combination has been widely explored, it remains unreported within the visible light spectrum. This study experimentally demonstrates a reflective meta-surface operating at $\lambda$ = 532 nm (green light), constructed from Ta$_2$O$_5$ and Sm$_2$O$_3$ nanorods with varying aspect ratios. The surface utilizes a magnetic resonance mechanism, and by adjusting the aspect ratio of the Ta$_2$O$_5$ nanorods, we successfully shifted the reflection phase across a full $2\pi$ range while maintaining a high reflection amplitude ($R$ = 0.50). Additionally, we observed that both phase and amplitude can be continuously adjusted simply by changing the Ta$_2$O$_5$ nanorod's aspect ratio. These findings confirm that this meta-surface design effectively fulfills the essential requirements for active light modulation and wavefront control, and it can be fabricated using standard nanofabrication techniques. Furthermore, we propose extending this design to an RGB meta-surface by incorporating appropriate magnetic ferrite layers, thereby enabling the generation of a complete color palette via phase modulation under white light illumination. Finally, the surface plasmon resonance method employed in this work is highly versatile for future hyperbolic material designs, which are crucial for achieving flat optics and superlenses. This research represents the initial step toward creating tunable meta-surfaces capable of color reproduction.

In this work, we broaden this perspective by incorporating the influence of transmedia information ecosystems. We achieve this by extending the Susceptible-Infected-Susceptible (SIS) model with a non-monotone infection rate function, which allows the function's shape to determine the existence and stability of system states. Through a change of variables, we transform the resulting nonlinear functional-differential equation into a Bellman equation. This reformulation enables the use of a fixed point argument to establish the existence and uniqueness of a mild solution, which can be interpreted as a regenerative process. Finally, we employ a square root ergodic theorem to demonstrate convergence to the stationary distribution expected in the long run. This approach allows us to calculate the average number of transmitters and the proportion of the population spreading falsehoods, offering insights that may help design strategies to limit misinformation spread. We validate our findings using real data from the George Floyd protests. Our study highlights the value of applying mathematical modeling to online misinformation, particularly by using an ecosystem-based model that captures the complexity of digital information environments. These methods can be extended to other problems, potentially informing solutions that address the challenges of the information age.

We introduce a stochastic version of the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick (SK) spin glass model on a bipartite graph, where spins for one set of vertices follow a Bernoulli distribution and those for the other set are arbitrary real numbers. By analyzing the free energy using large deviation principles, we demonstrate that the free energy converges to the same limit as the original SK model. This equivalence implies that key properties, such as the existence of a phase transition, remain identical in both models. Consequently, our framework opens pathways for investigating other well-established features of the original SK model, including the cancellation of self-interactions and the emergence of a replica symmetry breaking transition, which can be examined through the lens of the GoF interaction matrix. Validating these theoretical results with numerical simulations on geometric graphs is also discussed.

and provably efficient computational algorithm designed to identify suspicious events within high-frequency streams of complex data using only a limited number of human-labeled examples. Deploying accurate detection systems is essential for supporting human experts across various sectors of modern digital society; however, because such systems demand significant amounts of training data, collecting sufficient labeled examples is often prohibitively expensive. To address this challenge, HALFADO achieves its goals by integrating two key principles: first, it separates the processes of system deployment and model refinement, enabling the immediate deployment of an effective detector even when only a small number of labeled examples are available for later improvement of the model; second, it relies on the hypothesis that within any stream of complex data, the subset of suspicious events is both rare and distinct. Extensive experiments conducted on real-world datasets from two industry partners have demonstrated that HALFADO is a practical approach for detecting rare and distinct anomalies in data streams, achieving this with low overhead compared to alternative solutions. Although demonstrations offer a natural method for teaching robots, relying solely on movement trajectories fails to incorporate other modalities, such as audio cues from human instructors. To harness these audio signals effectively, it is essential to first identify the specific information they convey. This study characterizes the audio generated by human teachers performing multi-step manipulation tasks for a Sawyer robot by analyzing three feature categories: speech duration, prosodic expressiveness, and semantic content. By examining these features across four dimensions—demonstration types, audio usage instructions, subtasks, and demonstration speeds—the analysis reveals that while teachers use similar semantic words across different conditions, distinct audio and contextual features emerge. These findings highlight that human audio richly encodes demonstration attributes like speed and provides guidance on conflict resolution, offering a comprehensive source of teaching guidance beyond physical trajectories. Finally, we outline future directions for leveraging human audio in demonstration-based learning frameworks. Although these systems are increasingly common and favored across numerous contexts and by many users, their automated testing infrastructure lags behind that of traditional software, hindering efficient and effective development. Implementing an automated testing framework for conversational systems could enhance their quality by aiding developers in creating, running, and sustaining test cases. This paper presents our work-in-progress framework, implemented in Python, and explores key research challenges in building such tools for conversational agents. Specifically, we highlight difficulties related to defining expected behaviors, referred to as test oracles, and performing semantic comparisons of utterances. While our initial offerings are simple and imperfect, they serve as a resource for the research community to advance conversational agent testing. Additionally, we provide practical insights and lessons learned from deploying this tool in real-world scenarios. Ultimately, establishing an automated testing framework will facilitate the creation of dialogue systems that are not only technologically superior but also highly usable. We hope that our insights and the framework itself will inspire other engineers and researchers working on these systems. Although we do not offer definitive answers, we provide a comprehensive overview of the problems encountered and the solutions we have implemented.

Effective single-domain dialogue agents rely on a well-defined set of possible user utterances, or language acts. However, there is a scarcity of tools for testing multi-domain conversational agents. We introduce the Agent Testing Framework (ATF), which enables the test execution of natural language utterances against live dialogue systems deployed in multiple, distinct domains. Beyond offering practical implementation details and code snippets for building such testing infrastructure, we identify the core research challenges inherent to this endeavor. These include determining appropriate test oracle behaviors for both single and multi-domain contexts and implementing efficient similarity metrics for comparing agent and user responses. The ATF was developed to test Viserion, a virtual assistant capable of narrating Netflix content, finding news, and managing device settings.

We propose utilizing Paraphrase Identification (PI) tasks to solve the test oracle problem within an automated testing framework for multi-domain conversational agents. Each Paraphrase Identification subtask within Clutrr features a distinct theme, or domain; by training and evaluating a classifier on these subtasks, we can assess whether a live agent's behavior aligns with the domain it is currently interacting with. ### 1Introduction

Few-shot classification is designed to categorize novel classes using only a small set of support images. Despite significant progress over the past decade, the standard approach typically relies on simple mean or k-nearest neighbor (kNN) prototypes calculated from support data, which often results in suboptimal performance because these basic prototypes are highly vulnerable to outlier samples (Figure 1).

Existing methods attempt to mitigate this limitation by incorporating external memory, contrastive learning, or adaptive metric modules. For instance, RSN utilizes recursive similarity normalization to reduce over-fitting during novel class identification, while CoRSa maintains class-specific representations in external memory to classify seen classes. Subspace memory networks similarly preserve class-specific hyperplanes in external memory for efficient classification. Similarly, Prototypical Networks with Adaptation (PNA) applies contrastive loss to update in-memory prototypes so they remain discriminative for incoming classes.

To reduce overlap between classes' feature distributions, CORAL learns an overlap reduction transformation from support images, and CL learns class-level representations from them. Contrastast networks also employ a contrast adaptive module for the same purpose. However, because these methods optimize features rather than prototypes, they often underperform compared to techniques that directly target prototypes.

Recent iterations of projects like ProjectillE and CORA attempt to learn adaptive overlap reduction functions and robustness metrics, respectively, but the computational cost of applying these models to generate class-based representations from support images makes real-time application impractical.

Although our method differs conceptually and technically from these existing approaches, it shares the core objective of producing high-quality prototypes to enhance classification performance. Nevertheless, existing theoretical and practical frameworks for CDR often rely on the restrictive assumption of complete and noise-free domain-specific user data. This limitation is particularly problematic in real-world scenarios, where user profiles are frequently incomplete, contain errors, or are absent for most users. To address this, we investigate the impact of imperfect profiles on collaborative filtering-based multi-domain recommendation. Our analysis reveals that, to our knowledge, no current methods guarantee accuracy bounds for this specific problem. We derive an accuracy bound for profiles generated by a specific sampling algorithm and prove that linear combining of domain RBF networks yields an accuracy guarantee when profiles are missing for all users in a domain. Furthermore, we introduce Profile-Augmented Domain RBF (PA-RBF), a practical method that achieves an accuracy lower bound for profiles from any single domain and a regret bound for the overall system accuracy. Empirical results on real datasets confirm PA-RBF's efficacy, showing it outperforms state-of-the-art techniques by up to 68%. Recommender systems help individuals with limited interests or those new to a platform by leveraging the behavior of similar users. Ideally, these systems should assist new users even with minimal data, such as their demographic information. This paper examines cross-domain recommendation using very incomplete profiles and establishes an accuracy bound for such cases. We present an algorithm with a sublinear regret bound for a specific theoretical scenario and a linear regret bound for a more practical one. Results from Netflix and Last.fm datasets indicate the proposed method's significant potential, surpassing recent state-of-the-art approaches by as much as 80%. Code can be found at https://github.com/ahmdsh/CDCR. Index Terms: Cross domain recommendation, incomplete profiles, regret bound.

We address the challenge of recommending items to users with incomplete side information by formulating it as a bandit problem with matrix side information. This problem encompasses several recent cross-domain recommendation tasks as specific cases. We propose a linear cross-domain algorithm that exceeds the regret lower bound for the general problem and matches the sample complexity of recent state-of-the-art solutions for a particular setting. Our method is also evaluated on an e-commerce dataset. Index Terms: Online learning,

In practice, however, algorithms and software libraries like ConeCGAL typically rely on even smaller, often symmetric, subcones. This restriction arises because any parent cone can be decomposed into a direct sum of irreducible cones, which are considered the algebraic and geometric building blocks of convex optimization. We demonstrate that commonly used subcones fail to capture the maximal rank of matrices or the ranks of factors within a matrix factorization. Furthermore, the direct sum of two such subcones does not represent the rank of their matrix addition. Similarly, other properties definable via extended formulations using auxiliary variables may not be representable through extended formulations using auxiliary matrices. While the growth rate of the size of necessary extended formulations can be analyzed for irreducible cones like the nonnegative orthant and second-order cone, this is not guaranteed for their direct sums or for subcones such as the positive definite cone. Additionally, we note that irreducible cones do not encompass all relevant functions in analysis; for instance, no convex cone contains all nondecreasing functions defined on a directed set, nor does any irreducible cone contain all such functions as an element. It has long been possible to work with irreducible cones and their direct sums by employing constraints based on additional data types, such as matrices. However, this approach does not align with the use of extended formulations relying on function properties like monotonicity or convexity. Although this may seem like a minor technical detail compared to issues with approximations, inexactness, or computational cost with extended formulations using scalar auxiliary variables, the choice of algebraic structure is, in fact, paramount for correctly and efficiently formulating problems. We argue that irreducible cones and their direct sums are sufficient for accurately and effectively formulating any convex optimization problem, similar to how real numbers are sufficient for formulating any continuous optimization problem. This argument relies on a growth rate analysis for the rank of matrices within specific subcones, with an upper bound established as a significant contribution. Additionally, we observe that irreducible cones and their direct sums support efficient algorithms, particularly for factorizing matrices and updating determinants and inverses. Adopting this perspective on algebraic structure could simplify cone selection, enhance software design, and improve formulations and algorithms by leveraging matrix-based irreducible cones and their efficient arithmetic. Although various efforts have created reliable and scalable QC pipelines, generalizing these methods to new, unseen data remains challenging due to inherent biases in MRI information. This study evaluates the impact of MRI biases on modern deep learning-based automatic QC pipelines and proposes a method to enhance their robustness. The research analyzes over 10,000 MRI scans from three distinct cohorts to train and test a end-to-end pipeline for detecting corrupted images. The primary finding shows that an MRI-corruption detection model trained and tested exclusively within a single institution achieves a high mean average precision (MAP) of 0.85, but this MAP drops significantly to 0.35 when tested on data from a different institution. These results indicate that format biases, embedded in the k-space encoding and pre-processing of raw MRI data, severely hinder the generalization of deep learning-based QC models. To address this, the study introduces a novel approach using self-supervised feature extractors trained on institution-specific data to build robust corruption detection models that generalize to similar formats seen during training. The authors demonstrate that training and testing across institutions can yield a MAP of 0.80, representing a substantial improvement over cross-institutional maps ranging from 0.30 to 0.50. To the best of the authors' knowledge, this work presents one of the first evaluations of MRI format bias in deep learning-based QC and its mitigation. The code is available at https://github.com/AmirHamedani/MRI-Bias-and-Generalization.

The growing availability of multi-center MRI datasets has sparked significant interest in machine learning models for MRI quality control (QC). This paper introduces the first rigorous study of both corrupted image detection and MRI format bias using a dataset of 13,000 images from four centers. The authors confirm that these models generally achieve high performance on corrupted image detection when tested across different formats, with a MAP of 0.85. However, when testing across different formats, the MAP drops to 0.40. Employing the Codeassis package, we conducted comprehensive plane-wave based first-principles calculations. Deep detectors leverage scene context in distinct ways. This study categorizes object detectors into three groups based on their context utilization: those with no context (RCNN via input cropping), those with partial context (two-stage methods via featuremap cropping), and those with full context (single-stage methods without cropping). We systematically assess the impact of context across these detector categories by constructing a fully controlled dataset with varying contextual conditions and analyzing context usage in deep detectors. Furthermore, we evaluate the effects of progressively removing background and foreground elements on the MS COCO dataset. Our findings indicate that both single-stage and two-stage detectors inherently utilize context through their extensive receptive fields, suggesting that the optimal detector choice often depends on the specific application context. As a contribution to building more context-aware detectors, we release the comprehensive "ContextVar" dataset, which features images with artificially altered contexts. To demonstrate effective context utilization, we introduce the U^2Net, a novel two-step detector achieving full context usage. ContextVar ranks as the largest natural scene object detection dataset to date, containing over 120,000 images. On MS COCO, our method attains an Ap of 63.9%, significantly outperforming the current state-of-the-art Ap of 59.4%. Additionally, we provide an video demonstration of context usage. The code for our detector and dataset is available at https://github.com/zhengjia99/ContextVar.

Researchers aim to apply graph neural networks (GNNs) to model molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, as they can generalize across unseen chemical environments, potentially offering a computationally efficient alternative to MD for specific applications. However, accurately modeling complex many-body phenomena like the two-dimensional (2D) liquid-vapor interface remains an open challenge. We demonstrate that an isotropic bond-based GNN, capable of preserving the conservation laws essential for interface dynamics, can only marginally smooth out spurious currents at the 2D liquid-vapor interface of a macroscopic droplet within a evaporating windbox. These spurious currents exceed physical values by five to six orders of magnitude. To achieve an accurate and efficient representation of the 2D liquid-vapor interface, we propose employing a nonbonded particle representation. This approach not only accurately captures the physisorbed water structure at the interface but also maintains mass conservation to machine precision, all while using a coarse grid resolution relative to the molecular diameter. This approach represents the most significant improvement to date in GNN methods for simulating fluid–fluid interfaces, marking the first instance where such a model can accurately and efficiently represent an macroscopic liquid–vapor interface without needing to resolve it down to the molecular scale.

These controlled operations generate derivational ambiguities that the original Lambek Calculus and its pregroup variant fail to capture. Although proposals exist for interpreting extended Lambek Calculus compositionally within the compact closed category of FVect and linear maps, these approaches treat syntax-semantics mappings as ignoring the control modalities, thereby limiting their influence to syntax alone. Our objective is to elevate these modalities to first-class status within the vectorial interpretation. We achieve this by extending the semantic mapping target to a two-layered framework comprising a public domain for uncontrolled composition and a private domain for structured, controlled information. This private-to-public data migration is modeled using projection operators, which we term "reanalysis." To our knowledge, the proposed category of spaces and linear maps with reanalysis offers a comprehensive and economical account of natural language syntax. A practical application is demonstrated through an enhanced modeling of English using the Penn Treebank as empirical data. Furthermore, we illustrate how the framework captures phenomena such as verb raising and cliticization, which were unaccounted for in the initial linear model. The resulting public derivations align with the standard Lambek Calculus, yet the private data reveals novel insights into syntactic processes. Consequently, our model of controlled composition demonstrates that natural language syntax can be effectively described as a lambda calculus of first-class control operators. The updated linear syntactic model proves capable of documenting linguistic patterns like verb raising and cliticization, previously requiring ad-hoc adjustments to the lambda-calculus interpretation. We term the resulting system the Syntactic Calculus of Control, which exhibits a formal affinity with the Holic Calculus. The enhanced English syntax model utilizes a significantly more compact set of axiomatically defined category assignments compared to the raw grammatical facts of the language. These observations suggest that the syntactic structure of natural language constitutes a calculus of control akin to that found in the theoretical computer science of programming with first-class control. Finally, the system demonstrates that linguistic phenomena classically attributed to phrasal grammar, such as verb raising and cliticization in English, can be explained through a purely word-based grammar of control.

We present an algorithm to identify a rationalizable correlated equilibrium (CE) in polynomial time, a representational complexity, and a communication complexity that are both polynomial in the size of the extensive-form game tree. This result is significant because, for rationalizable CEs in extensive-form games, the polynomial time complexity is considered optimal; furthermore, it is well-established that no such CE exists in potential classes of these games (such as quantal response, logit, or linear) when the number of players is part of the input. Our representation relies on a correlation device depicted as a directed, weighted, rooted tree, which is equivalent to a set of conditional distributions. This structure is particularly powerful for multiagent learning, as it enables a player to execute a rationalizable strategy by maintaining only a correlated subpolicy, rather than the full conditional distribution, to fulfill the equilibrium's requirements. These algorithms are broadly applicable to various multiagent learning contexts, such as repeated games with bandit or full information, multiagent reinforcement learning, and cooperative pathfinding. It is worth noting that while a similar outcome was recently achieved by Shaffer et al. (2023) specifically for CCE in matrix games, their representation schema and underlying complexities differ substantially from ours.

To address the high computation cost, we propose an approximate return computation method leveraging Graph Neural Networks (GNN) to replace traditional dynamic programming approaches like Bellman backups. For handling the system's transition dynamics, we design a message-passing network, specifically a CNN utilized as a weight generator within the GNN architecture. This message-passing network approach is employed to approximate both the baseline and the probability distribution of the trace. We implement these two approximations on two real-world simulation tasks: an inverted pendulum and a boomerang. The results demonstrate that our approximate actor-critic method utilizing a GNN achieves performance comparable to the exact actor-critic method while significantly reducing computation time. Additionally, the paper includes a detailed description of the GNN's internal working mechanism, which can be applied to model non-linear system dynamics. Finally, our method is tested on two environment modification tasks, which assess the algorithm's sensitivity to shifts in transition dynamics.

In reinforcement learning for complex stochastic systems, an actor-critic approach is used where the actor updates the policy via the score function and the critic provides a baseline (the state value function) to reduce variance. However, in multi-factor systems, accurately estimating the baseline and transition dynamics is difficult and computationally expensive. We approximate the return using a recurrent message-passing network, specifically a CNN acting as a weight generator for the recurrent component. This allows the network to estimate the baseline directly from the returns of the previous iteration rather than through direct return calculation or Bellman backups, thus modeling the transition dynamics implicitly. We evaluate this approach on two modified classical control tasks: tracking and swing-up. Experiments show that our method achieves performance comparable to the exact actor-critic method while significantly saving computation time. Furthermore, testing on a modified wind-up archery task confirms the method's robustness against perturbations in transition dynamics. The message-passing network architecture is also applicable to other dynamic factor scenarios, such as those found in systems with hierarchical transition dynamics.

This study examines the security of an intelligent reflecting surface (IRS)-assisted cognitive radio (CR) communication system. Our numerical results demonstrate that the proposed RMT-based optimization significantly surpasss suboptimal techniques, including both suboptimal and optimal power allocation strategies found in recent literature.

We examine the geometric characteristics of topological solitons arising from scalar fields with both $\mathbb{S}^1$-invariant and general potentials. It is shown that when the potential is $\mathbb{S}^1$-invariant, topological stability is guaranteed only for kinks located at the field's critical points. Conversely, in cases where the symmetry is not $\mathbb{S}^1$-invariant, topological stability arises from kinks positioned between critical points. This finding offers new insights into topological solitons within topdown cosmological models. We establish that mini-balls and mini-balls with cavities are unstable, whereas mini-balls with cavities and anti-balls exhibit topological stability. These stable configurations may serve as viable models for baryons and other massive particles within topdown cosmology.

To detect UHE photons, one must either measure their flux or their interaction length. Given the sparse nature of the flux, determining interaction length is the more feasible approach. We employ the \textit{UHEstar} module to simulate cascades initiated by UHE photons across various galactic distances, incorporating realistic sources and ISM distributions. These simulations will enable the CRAB detector to measure interaction lengths, thereby offering an alternative to direct observation for finding UHE photons.

To investigate specific energy losses, \textit{UHEstar} can calculate the total energy lost to pions and gamma rays over a specified distance. This functionality is essential for determining interaction lengths at energies where the mean free path exceeds a galactic diameter.

To study cosmic ray spectra, \textit{UHEstar} can simulate crystals of specific masses (up to 10^6 GeV/c^2) at distinct galactic locations. It accounts for the specified source distribution and can be adapted to include other injection mechanisms. These simulations align with existing measurements from the Auger and Telescope Array observatories. Furthermore, \textit{UHEstar} offers the potential to analyze data from the future Southern Wideband Array.

In summary, this paper defines an framework for creating efficient CRDTs, introduces a practical implementation using that framework, and proves its effectiveness in both heap and set implementations. We analyzed 1.15 million Genomic Superstructures (GSS) to determine their utility for associating genetic variants with complex traits and understanding functional genomics. We found that the optimal GSS annotation depends on the specific GWAS question being addressed. For example, brain-specific GSS regions were strongly associated with neuropsychiatric traits, whereas GSS elements linked to mRNA splicing were associated with a broader range of complex traits. Analyzing annotations from multiple Assay for Transposase-Accessible Chromatin (ATAC) sources in mice yielded higher explanatory power for complex traits than using any single source separately. We propose a general framework for evaluating and selecting appropriate annotations for GWAS variant interpretation, which can be applied to other data types beyond those tested here, such as protein structures, chromatin interactions, and supergenes. Adopting this systematic approach could enhance our understanding of complex traits, ultimately benefiting disease prevention, diagnosis, and treatment. Associate authors: Alexander V. Gusev, PhD, and Nicholas K. Schork, MD, MPH. Background: Although annotation data are valuable for interpreting GWAS findings, choosing the most relevant set of annotations (e.g., for pathway analysis) remains a challenge. While previous research has often focused on human annotations, many functional genomic assays are more robust in mice; thus, methods to select appropriate annotations are needed across both species. Results: ATAC-seam analysis was employed to construct mouse gene and enhancer annotations for various cell types and tissues, which were then evaluated for their ability to explain complex trait associations using 10,180 mouse quantitative traits from the International Mouse Phenotype Database (IMPD). This analysis revealed that the best enhancer annotations are those with the strongest link to complex traits in their native assay context. Furthermore, across both mice and humans, annotations most informative for complex traits are those most closely tied to basic cellular processes. While most GSS annotations for gene structures were pre-existing, constructing optimal annotations required combining multiple ATAC-seam-enhancer annotations. Conclusions: Constructing and selecting annotations most relevant to complex traits is essential for interpreting GWAS results. The ATAC-seam method offers a framework for assessing and building such annotations, a resource particularly valuable given the increasing availability of high-quality multi-omics data from model organisms. These systems are defined by wide minor axes (larger than the light travel time of radio emission) that exhibit significant linear polarization. We analyze the radio emission mechanism in these AgB galaxies by leveraging their unique constraint: their large minor axes imply that any emission from the central engine (the black hole) arrives as incoherent radiation. Consequently, the observed polarization must result from scattering by intermediate structures, such as the scattering screen located within the broad-line region (BLR). By applying the conservation of Stokes parameters, we calculate the electron number density of the screen using the intrinsic polarization of the jet, the scattered polarization, and the electron density of the gas host galaxy. Our results indicate that the mean density of these screens is at least an order of magnitude higher than previously assumed, although the scatter is considerable. This finding offers a new perspective on AgB galaxies and their utility in investigating the gas dynamics of host galaxies. Additionally, the derived screen density suggests that future high-precision polarization observations of AgB systems using VLBI could probe the morphology of the electron distribution inside the BLR. We argue that the specific requirements for this method are not unexpected in AgB galaxies and that the derived screen density is consistent with recent volatile disk models. The density of these screens is also comparable to that found in other scattering sources, such as 3C273 and 3C279. Finally, the total mass of these screens is at most a small fraction ($<10^{-3}$) of the mass of the central black hole. The total mass limit is actually much smaller ($<10^{-5}$) if these screens are not the primary scattering component in the AGN. Contextually, the total mass of AgB screens is lower than that of ultra-faint dwarf galaxies ($<10^{-2}$) and significantly lower than the gas halo mass limit derived from the rotation curves of host galaxies. By employing approximate adiabatic invariants, we extend the classical equal-area method into equal-integral form for both shocks and non-shock waves. Our analysis derives generalized shock equations suitable for any transonic, one-dimensional flow, which we apply to acoustic shocks traveling through a contact discontinuity separating two adiabats. Assuming the front of an acoustically driven shock wave train represents a genuine shock, we determine the number of periods in the resulting "saw-tooth" profile based on the acoustic pulse's amplitude. This approach is applied to pulsating stars, predicting that super-Eddington acoustic shocks generate "type-I" pulsations characterized by rapid brightening followed by a gradual, damped decline. Additionally, these high-amplitude shocks can drive intense mass ejections, causing the stellar brightness to peak just as the pulse traverses the star. We examine how the initial pulse shape, surface boundary conditions, and the coupling between shock ejection and mass loss influence the light curve. Finally, our findings are compared against the classic "starquake" model of type-II pulsations, where light curves are defined by the shock crossing the surface (type-I) or the formation of an "opacity shell" behind a direct shock (type-II). The observed distinction between these supernova types may stem from the initial disturbance caused by the core collapse or explosion. We suggest that the "opacity shell" is generated by a wave train rather than a shock and Spherically Symmetric Supernova simulations support this "opacity shell" concept. Although the resulting light curves, colors, and mass-loss profiles differ significantly between the two scenarios, both predict that the shock eventually becomes subsonic in the post-shock frame, allowing the equal-area method to apply. These structures are frequently depicted in a two-tiered layout, where each entity set is shown as a collection of vertices aligned on one of two parallel horizontal lines, and their relationships are illustrated by edges linking corresponding vertices across the lines. A primary goal in creating such visualizations is to reduce edge crossings; however, minimizing crossings is computationally demanding and often yields drawings with so many intersections that they compromise readability. This work examines a recent method for eliminating crossings by splitting vertices, aiming to identify the minimum number of vertices that must be split to achieve a planar representation. We demonstrate that deciding whether a planar drawing is achievable by splitting at most $k$ vertices is $\mathcal{NP}$-complete for any $k \geq 2$. Furthermore, while prior research has established that $3k$ vertices are sufficient for a planar drawing when $k$ vertices are split, we prove that $4k+1$ is the tightest possible upper bound. Additionally, we introduce an iterative algorithm capable of finding a planar drawing without vertex splitting that plans for at most $4k$ split vertices, where $k$ is a user-defined parameter. Notably, this algorithm runs at least $2.87$ times faster than the previous state-of-the-art approach. Empirical tests on both synthetic and real-world datasets indicate that the proposed method produces drawings with significantly fewer crossings, typically roughly twice as many as the best existing solutions.

Our approach utilizes a hybrid zero dynamics (HZD) framework to generate reference trajectories, with feedback derived from linearization around these trajectories. The ASSURE platform, detailed in [Yi20], features six thrusters positioned above the feet, enabling thrust generation during the swing-leg phase and during foot-flat transitions.

To overcome this, Random Fourier Features (RFF) were introduced to approximate kernel functions using randomized Fourier features, enabling scalability. Despite its popularity, RFF has notable limitations: because it samples features from a distribution independent of the training data, it demands a large number of feature dimensions to match the performance of kernelized classifiers, a requirement that scales with dataset size. This paper introduces Pseudo Random Fourier Features (PRFF), a data-dependent kernel approximation technique designed to minimize feature dimensions and enhance predictive performance. In summary, PRFF approximates positive definite kernels more effectively than RFF, offering a scalable solution for kernel learning on large-scale data.

Multivariate extreme value analysis often relies on the assumption of asymptotic independence between variables, meaning that large events in one location do not necessarily lead to large events in another. We utilize a regression model for $\eta$ based on the spectral dependence parameter from the class of spectral representation models (SRM). # Introduction

Humans effortlessly assign meanings to words, a fundamental skill for language comprehension; for example, the term "bright" has multiple interpretations. While context usually allows humans to determine the appropriate meaning, NLP models frequently fail at this task, a problem known as Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD). Although numerous models and benchmarks exist for WSD, a consensus model has not yet emerged (Huang et al., 2019; Mudge et al., 2019).

# Background

WSD involves determining the specific meaning of a word within a sentence, such as distinguishing between the definitions of "date" as "sweet fruit" or "an appointment." This challenge has been widely investigated, with various models and benchmarks available. We align with the framework and data used by Huang et al. (2019).

Graphene magic-angle twisted bilayer exhibits unexpected strong correlations when a global twist angle is introduced, leading to the observation of various strongly correlated phases through experimental band-filling sequences. By leveraging a recently developed tight-binding model that accurately captures the single-particle band structures of MAG, we perform a comprehensive finite-temperature many-body analysis using a combination of cluster dynamical mean-field theory and quantum Monte Carlo simulations. Our study focuses on the interplay between electron-electron interactions and electron-phonon couplings within the two-flavor Hubbard model on an octagonal lattice. We map out a three-dimensional phase diagram exploring the influence of electron doping and strong coupling on the normal-state phase structure. We successfully reproduce multiple experimentally observed phases, including charge density waves, electron-phonon bound states, and half-metallic phases. Furthermore, by varying filling and band parameters, we uncover new phases in undoped and hole-doped systems, such as charge order, spin density waves, and a fully polarized ferromagnetic phase. These results highlight the critical role of the twisted boundary condition in MAG's strong correlation physics and provide a robust theoretical framework for future experimental and theoretical inquiries into this magic-angle system.
